stem: Find which of the following matrices are invertible: (i) \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 4 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\)  (ii) \(B = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & \sin\theta \\ -\sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix}\)  (iii) \(C = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 & 2 \\ 3 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\)
solution:
(i) As \(|A| = \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 4 & 2 \end{vmatrix} = 0\), \(A\) is singular and hence \(A\) is not invertible.
(ii) As \(|B| = \begin{vmatrix} \cos\theta & \sin\theta \\ -\sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{vmatrix} = \cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta = 1 \neq 0\), \(B\) is nonsingular, \(B\) is invertible.
(iii) \(|C| = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 3 & 2 \\ 3 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \end{vmatrix} = -12 \neq 0\), \(C\) is nonsingular and hence \(C\) is invertible.

As \(|A| = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{vmatrix} = -2\), \(|A| \neq 0\) so \(A^{-1}\) exists.
Let \(AA^{-1} = I\) (Here we can use only row transformation).
Using \(R_2 \to R_2 - 3R_1\), \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix} A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\) becomes \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & -2 \end{bmatrix} A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).
Using \(-\tfrac{1}{2}R_2\) we get \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ \tfrac{3}{2} & -\tfrac{1}{2} \end{bmatrix}\).
Using \(R_1 \to R_1 - 2R_2\), we get \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 1 \\ \tfrac{3}{2} & -\tfrac{1}{2} \end{bmatrix}\).
\(\therefore A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 1 \\ \tfrac{3}{2} & -\tfrac{1}{2} \end{bmatrix}\)

stem: Find the inverse of \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 2 & 6 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 5 \end{bmatrix}\) by using elementary row transformations.
solution:
Consider \(|A| = 1 \neq 0\) so \(A^{-1}\) exists.
Consider \(AA^{-1} = I\), i.e. \(\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 2 & 6 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 5 \end{bmatrix} A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).
Use \(R_1 \leftrightarrow R_2\): \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 2 & 6 \\ 2 & 2 & 5 \end{bmatrix} A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).
Use \(R_2 \to R_2 - 3R_1\) and \(R_3 \to R_3 - 2R_1\): \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).
Use \(R_2 \to -R_2\): \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).
Use \(R_1 \to R_1 - R_2\): \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 & 0 \\ -1 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).
Use \(R_1 \to R_1 - 2R_3\): \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & -2 \\ -1 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).
\(\therefore A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & -2 \\ -1 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\)

stem: Find the inverse of \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 & 3 \\ 1 & 4 & 3 \\ 1 & 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\) by elementary column transformation.
solution:
As \(A^{-1}\) is required by column transformations we consider \(A^{-1}A = I\), i.e. \(A^{-1} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 & 3 \\ 1 & 4 & 3 \\ 1 & 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).
Using \(C_2 \to C_2 - 3C_1\) and \(C_3 \to C_3 - 3C_1\): \(A^{-1} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -3 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).
Use \(C_1 \to C_1 - C_2\): \(A^{-1} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & -3 & -3 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).
Use \(C_1 \to C_1 - C_3\): \(A^{-1} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 7 & -3 & -3 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).
\(\therefore A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 7 & -3 & -3 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\)

stem: Find the co-factors of the elements of \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\).
If \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -2 \\ 4 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\), then find \(A^{-1}\) by the adjoint method.
If \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 & 1 \\ -1 & 2 & -1 \\ 1 & -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\), find \(A^{-1}\) by the adjoint method.

solution:
For \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\):
\(A_{11} = (-1)^{1+1}(4) = 4\), \(A_{12} = (-1)^{1+2}(3) = -3\), \(A_{21} = (-1)^{2+1}(2) = -2\), \(A_{22} = (-1)^{2+2}(1) = 1\).
\(\text{adj}\,A = \begin{bmatrix} A_{11} & A_{21} \\ A_{12} & A_{22} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & -2 \\ -3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).
\(\therefore A(\text{adj}\,A) = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 4 & -2 \\ -3 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 \end{bmatrix}\)  ...(i)
\((\text{adj}\,A)A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & -2 \\ -3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 \end{bmatrix}\)  ...(ii)
And \(|A|\,I = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{vmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = (-2)\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 \end{bmatrix}\)  ...(iii)
From (i), (ii) and (iii) we get, \(A(\text{adj}\,A) = (\text{adj}\,A)A = |A|\,I\).
